title: Most Classes Before Their Deadlines
statement:
You get a list of online classes. Class i is classes[i] = [duration, lastDay]: it takes duration full days of study and must be finished by the end of day lastDay.

You start on day 1, study one class at a time, and do not switch until it is done. A class you start must be finished in time, or it does not count. Return the largest number of classes you can complete.

examples.why: [3, 4] ends on day 3 and [2, 5] on day 5. Adding [4, 6] would end on day 9. No three fit in 6 days, since together they need 9.
Taking the 5-day class first blocks the rest. Skipping it lets the three 2-day classes end on days 2, 4 and 6.
The class needs 3 days but must be done by day 2.

hints: If you already know which classes you will take, in which order should you take them?
Earliest deadline first is always a safe order. So walk the classes sorted by lastDay and decide which ones to keep.

Add each class and its duration to a running total. If the total passes this class's lastDay, drop the longest class taken so far (a max-heap finds it). Dropping the longest frees the most time while losing only one class.

explain.intuition:
First, ordering: for a fixed set of classes, doing them in order of deadline works whenever any order works. So sort by lastDay and only decide which classes to keep.

Go through the sorted classes and take each one, adding its duration to the day count. If that overshoots the current deadline, one class has to go, and the best one to drop is the longest taken so far, possibly the one just added. You still have the same number of classes as before this step, but you end as early as possible, which leaves the most room for everything later. A max-heap of durations gives the longest one in O(log n). This "take it, then drop the worst if over budget" trick shows up in many scheduling problems.
steps: Keep a max-heap of chosen durations and day = 0.
For each class: push its duration and add it to day.
If day > lastDay, pop the largest duration from the heap and subtract it from day.
pitfalls: Skipping a class that does not fit instead of swapping it for a longer one. In the second example that gives 2 instead of 3.
Sorting by duration. The shortest class may have a far-away deadline while a longer one is urgent.
Checking the deadline before adding the new class. Push first, then drop the longest; the longest may be the new class itself.

solutions.title: Try every subset
solutions.idea: For every subset, sort it by deadline and check that every class finishes on time. Keep the largest feasible subset.

solutions.title: Deadline order with a max-heap
solutions.idea: Take classes in deadline order. Whenever the schedule runs late, drop the longest class taken so far.

followups: Each class also has a value and you want the most total value, not the most classes. Why does the heap greedy fail, and what replaces it?
Return the actual list of classes in the order you would take them.
